words.meaning: One online application that many US colleges share. You enter your details, your activities and one personal essay once, then answer each college's own questions.
words.forYou: Check whether each college uses it: MIT has its own application.

words.meaning: Applying early, usually by 1 November, for a decision in December, without promising to attend.
words.forYou: You can still compare offers in the spring.

words.meaning: An early round that does not bind you to attend, but limits where else you may apply early. Harvard uses it.
words.forYou: Read each college's rule before you apply early anywhere else.

words.meaning: A binding early round: if you are admitted, you must attend and withdraw your other applications.
words.forYou: A college usually releases you if the aid it offers is not enough, so read its rule before you apply.

words.meaning: The main round, usually closing around 1 January, with decisions by the end of March.
words.forYou: Most of your list will be in this round.

words.meaning: The college decides on your application without looking at whether you need aid.
words.forYou: On its own it promises no money. Look for need-blind for international students together with meeting full need; many colleges are need-blind only for US citizens.

words.meaning: Your need for aid can affect the decision, often because the aid budget is limited.
words.forYou: Some need-aware colleges still meet the full need of every student they admit.

words.meaning: The college pays the gap between its price and what it works out your family can pay.
words.forYou: Need is the college's own calculation, not your family's estimate.

words.meaning: Money given for achievement, whatever your family earns.
words.forYou: Some colleges give none: Princeton's aid is all based on need.

words.meaning: A college's full yearly price before aid: tuition, fees, housing, food, books, personal costs and travel.
words.forYou: Compare colleges by this, not by tuition alone.

words.meaning: College Board's aid form, which many private colleges use to work out your need.
words.forYou: It costs money for each college you send it to, and international applicants usually pay.

words.meaning: Permission to apply without paying the application fee.
words.forYou: Ask for one if the fee is hard for your family; many colleges grant them to international students.

words.meaning: You may send SAT or ACT scores, but you do not have to.
words.forYou: Optional is not the same as ignored. Send a score if it helps your application.

words.meaning: The part of the Common App where you list up to 10 activities, each with a short description.
words.forYou: Family duties and paid work count as activities.

words.meaning: One essay of 250 to 650 words that goes to every college you apply to on the Common App.
words.forYou: Write it yourself, in your own voice.

words.meaning: Each college's own extra questions, added to the Common App.
words.forYou: Harvard asks five short ones.

words.meaning: A letter from a teacher or school official about you and your work.
words.forYou: Ask your teachers early, well before your first deadline.

words.meaning: A report your school sends with your grades from the first half of your final year.
words.forYou: Your grades keep counting after you apply.

words.meaning: The main subject of a US degree, usually chosen in the first two years.
words.forYou: You can explore before you decide.

words.meaning: The last day to accept an offer. Harvard's is 1 May.
words.forYou: Each college sets its own, so check yours.

words.meaning: A payment that holds your place after you accept an offer.
words.forYou: Ask each university whether it is refunded if your visa is refused.

words.meaning: The document a US school sends you so you can apply for the F-1 student visa.
words.forYou: The school issues it only after you show how you will pay.

words.meaning: A US government fee every new F-1 student pays after the I-20 arrives and before the visa interview.
words.forYou: Keep the receipt for your interview.

words.meaning: The US student visa for full-time study.
words.forYou: For Bangladeshi citizens it can be valid for up to 60 months.

words.meaning: The online visa application form you fill in before you book your interview.
words.forYou: Bring its confirmation page to the interview.

words.meaning: The part of US law an officer uses to refuse a visa when not satisfied that you qualify, including that you will leave after your studies.
words.forYou: It is not permanent: you can apply again and show what has changed.

words.meaning: Extra checks after the interview. The State Department counts the case as a refusal under section 221(g) until the checks finish.
words.forYou: Leave spare time before your flight. If a later form asks whether you were ever refused a US visa, this counts.

words.meaning: Permission to work in the USA after graduating, for up to 12 months, longer for science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees.
words.forYou: The rules may change: large new fees have been proposed.

words.meaning: Evidence that the money for your studies is available, such as bank statements and aid letters.
words.forYou: It must really be yours to use. Never borrow money only to show it: false documents can lead to a refusal.

words.meaning: One application on Studyinfo for up to six programmes; you can accept only one place.
words.forYou: One fee covers every application for the same term.

words.meaning: The official site where you apply to Finnish universities.
words.forYou: Apply there yourself.

words.meaning: A Finnish university focused on practical, work-related degrees.
words.forYou: Many choose students with the International UAS Exam.

words.meaning: Permission to live in Finland for your studies, applied for online and confirmed in person.
words.forYou: Bangladeshi applicants prove their identity at the Finland Application Centre in New Delhi.

words.meaning: Türkiye's government scholarship: tuition, a monthly stipend, housing, health insurance, a Turkish course and a university place.
words.forYou: Applicants must be under 21.

words.meaning: An entrance exam some Turkish universities accept from students from abroad, instead of the SAT.
words.forYou: It can be taken in Dhaka.

words.meaning: A year of English before the degree, for students who do not yet meet the English requirement.
words.forYou: It does not count towards the degree, so it adds time and fees.

words.meaning: Official stamps on a copy of your certificate from Bangladesh's Ministry of Education and Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
words.forYou: Pathway's plan allows up to 4 weeks for it.

words.meaning: The agency that handles student passes for Malaysia.
words.forYou: You or your university applies on the EMGS portal, so ask your university which it does.

words.meaning: The approval you need before you can enter Malaysia as a student.
words.forYou: It is valid for 6 months.

words.meaning: The permission that lets you stay in Malaysia as a student.
words.forYou: It is usually issued for up to a year at a time, then renewed.

words.meaning: The identity card Malaysia gives international students.
An online arrival form you fill in within the three days before you arrive.
A course of about a year before a degree, for students whose school results do not give direct entry.
words.forYou: It adds time and fees, but leads into the degree.

words.meaning: A university's written offer of a place, which you need for the visa or pass and for paying fees from Bangladesh.
words.forYou: Check whether it has conditions you still have to meet.

words.meaning: The units a New Zealand degree is counted in.
words.forYou: Victoria charges tuition for each point.

words.meaning: The money for living costs you must show for the New Zealand student visa.
New Zealand's points for Cambridge International A and AS level grades. 120 points is the usual entry level.
words.forYou: An A* at A level is worth 140 points.

words.meaning: A shared scale from A1 to C2 that describes how well you use a language. Each English test owner maps its scores to it.
words.forYou: Use it to compare tests roughly.

words.meaning: IELTS's word for a score: both each part, such as writing, and the overall result.
words.forYou: Many universities set a minimum for the overall score and for each part.

words.meaning: A table from a test owner showing roughly equal scores on two tests.
words.forYou: A comparison only: universities use the test you took.

words.meaning: An average of your grades as points. Bangladesh's HSC GPA is out of 5.
words.forYou: Report it as printed; do not convert it yourself.

words.meaning: The highest A level grade, above A.
words.forYou: It is worth 140 points on New Zealand's tariff.

words.meaning: Grades your school expects you to get, used before your final results.
words.forYou: Some universities refuse them: Bilkent does not evaluate them.

words.meaning: A bank service for sending tuition and living costs abroad, opened with your offer letter.
words.forYou: Banks charge their own fees for it.

words.meaning: Bangladesh's national ID card with a chip.
words.forYou: IELTS accepts it; TOEFL, PTE and the Duolingo English Test do not.

words.meaning: A police certificate showing your record, needed for some visas.
words.forYou: Apply online; it can take weeks.

words.meaning: How many taka one unit of another currency costs.
words.forYou: Your bank's rate for students is usually a little above Bangladesh Bank's.

words.meaning: A private company's ranking of universities.
words.forYou: There is no official ranking of US universities.
